row.name: Pumamarka, San Sebastián
row.description: Pumamarka (Aymara and Quechua: puma meaning "cougar" and marka meaning "village", i.e. "puma village") is an archaeological park in Peru's Cusco Region, situated in the San Sebastián District on the left bank of the Pumamarka River [1]. The site was declared a National Cultural Heritage (Patrimonio Cultural) of Peru by the National Institute of Culture [1] [2].

row.name: Biannus
row.description: Biannus or Biannos, or Biennus or Biennos, also Bienna, was an inland town and polis of ancient Crete [1]. It appears in the list of 22 cities of Crete of the sixth-century Byzantine geographer Hierocles [1]. According to the Stadiasmus Maris Magni, it was 170 stadia from Hierapytna and 270 stadia from Leben [1]. The contest of Otus and Ephialtes with Ares is said to have taken place near this city [1]. From this violent conflict the city is said to have derived its name [1]. The town minted coins in the Hellenistic period, some of which survive [1]. Its site is located near modern Khorakia, Ano Viannos, a hill northwest of modern Viannos, where remains have been found from the Orientalizing period to Roman times [1].

row.name: Roddenbury Hillfort
row.description: Roddenbury Hillfort is a univallate Iron Age hillfort in the parish of Selwood, Somerset [1]. It is a Scheduled Monument and it was on the Heritage at Risk Register in 2011 [1]. The site covers 0.84 hectares [1].

row.name: Helorus
row.description: Helorus (modern Eloro) was an ancient Greek colony of Syracuse founded in the late 8th century BC on the southeast coast of Sicily, connected to its mother city by the Via Elorina [1] [2] [3] [4]. Major discoveries include the Colonna Pizzuta, a 10.5-metre monumental column from the 3rd century BC [2] [5]. The city fell to Rome in 214 BC during the Second Punic War [1] [6].

row.name: Tregele
row.description: Tregele is a small village in northern Anglesey, Wales, near which stands the Llanfechell Cromlech [1]. Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age rock art was discovered on one of the monument's stones in 2004-2005 by Dr. George Nash [2] [3]. The site sits within a distinctive prehistoric burial-ritual landscape alongside the Meini Hirion stone group and the Llanfechell Standing Stone [2] [3]. The cromlech remains unscheduled and lacks formal heritage protection [2].

row.name: Walton Common
row.description: Walton Common is a 25.5 hectare biological Site of Special Scientific Interest near the village of Walton in Gordano, North Somerset [1]. The site has two saucer-shaped round barrows from the Bronze Age, and the Walton Common banjo enclosure, a banjo enclosure from the late Iron Age that may be a univallate hillfort [1].

row.name: Markušica
row.description: Markusica is a village in Vukovar-Syrmia County in eastern Croatia, located south of the river Vuka and northwest of Vinkovci [1] [2]. A Scordisci archaeological site dating to the Late La Tene culture was excavated here during rescue excavations in the 1970s and 1980s [1] [2]. The site formed part of the broader Scordisci settlement network in the Vinkovci area [1]. The landscape is characterized by Pannonian Basin plains with agricultural fields [1].

row.name: Church of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, Ras
row.description: The Church of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul (Petrova Crkva) is the oldest intact church in Serbia, situated on a hill of Ras, the medieval capital of the Serbian Grand Principality, in Novi Pazar [1]. Excavations beneath the floor unearthed Greek sculptures and black-figure pottery from the 7th-6th centuries BC, and a 5th-century BC princely grave with gold-silver jewellery [1] [2]. Stefan Nemanja, founder of the Nemanjic dynasty, was baptised here [1] [3]. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Stari Ras and Sopocani, inscribed in 1979 [1] [4] [5].

row.description: A 5th Dynasty double tomb on the southeastern edge of the Abusir necropolis in Egypt [1]. The eastern tomb measures 27.7 x 21.5 m and the western 21.7 x 15.7 m, with walls inclined at approximately 78 degrees [1]. The complex lacked a traditional mortuary temple [1]. Both tombs had north-south descending passages leading to burial chambers [1].

row.name: Villa of Diomedes
row.description: The Villa of Diomedes is an ancient Roman villa near Pompeii [1]. It is located outside the walls of Pompeii on the Via dei Sepolcri to the Gate of Herculaneum [1]. It was excavated from 1771 to 1774 by Francesco La Vega [1]. It was named after Marcus Arrius Diomedes, whose grave is opposite the entrance to the villa, though it is not clear that it was in fact his villa [1]. The villa sits just outside the city walls on the north side of Pompeii [1]. It is around 3500 square meters [1]. The garden side of the building faces what would have been the ancient coast line to the East [1]. The villa is on two levels [1].

row.name: Keal Cotes
row.description: Keal Cotes is a small village in East Lindsey, Lincolnshire, England, with archaeological evidence of Roman occupation from the 1st to 4th century AD [1]. A 1960s excavation and field walk uncovered tessellated mosaic floor tiles and roof tiles indicating a substantial Roman villa or high-status Romano-British farmhouse [1]. Centuries of agricultural activity have plowed out further excavation possibilities, though cropmark outlines of an extensive dwelling remain visible in aerial photographs [1].

row.name: Megarian Treasury, Olympia
row.description: The Megarian Treasury at Olympia, was an ancient Greek building, located in the sanctuary of Olympia, which held votive offerings of the Greek city-state of Megara [1]. The Megarian Treasury was mainly built from limestone, with the roof made of terracotta tiles [1]. The building was adorned with several statues, including limestone reliefs and carvings in cedarwood [1]. Due to its architectural styling, both the statues and the building itself are believed by archaeologists to originate from the 500s BCE [1].

row.name: Stobno, Lower Silesian Voivodeship
row.description: Stobno is a village in Gmina Wolow, Lower Silesian Voivodeship, southwestern Poland, with settlement dating back to prehistoric times [1]. Archaeological sites from the Bronze Age and the Early Middle Ages have been identified in the area [1]. The earliest written mention of the village dates from 1259, when it was part of Piast-ruled Poland, a domain it had belonged to since the late 10th century [1] [2]. The village lies approximately 7 km south of Wolow [3].

row.name: Mawk'allaqta, Sandia
row.description: Mawk'allaqta (also Mawk'a Llaqta) is an archaeological settlement in the Puno Region of southeastern Peru, located in the Sandia Province within the Sandia District [1] [2] [3]. In recognition of its historical and cultural significance, Mawk'allaqta was declared a National Cultural Heritage (Patrimonio Cultural) of Peru by the National Institute of Culture [1].

row.name: Marpa, Peru
row.description: Marpa is a ruined pre-Hispanic town in the Cotahuasi Canyon in southern Peru's Andes, one of the world's deepest canyons at around 3,400 metres deep [1] [2]. The ruins straddle both sides of the river [2]. The Inca road through the canyon may follow an older route built by the Wari culture (c. 500-900 AD) [1].

row.name: Pyramid of Amenemhat I
row.description: The Pyramid of Amenemhat I is an Egyptian burial structure built at el-Lisht by the founder of the Twelfth Dynasty, who moved the capital from Thebes to nearby Itj-tawy [1] [2]. The pyramid now stands at approximately 20 m due to poor construction, quarrying, and tomb robberies [2]. Its core was made of small rough limestone blocks filled with sand, debris, and mudbrick, and notably reused blocks from earlier royal monuments [1] [2] [3].

row.name: Keilor Archaeological Site
row.description: The Keilor archaeological site was among the first places to demonstrate the antiquity of Aboriginal occupation of Australia when a cranium, unearthed in 1940, was found to be nearly 15,000 years old [1] [2]. Subsequent investigations of Pleistocene alluvial terraces revealed hearths about 31,000 years BP, making Keilor one of the earliest sites of human habitation in Australia [1] [2]. Remains of megafauna suggest a possible association with Aboriginal hunting [1] [2].

row.name: Garni Temple
row.description: The Garni Temple is a classical colonnaded structure in the village of Garni, in central Armenia, around 30 km east of Yerevan [1]. Built in the Ionic order, it is the best-known structure and symbol of pre-Christian Armenia [1]. Considered an eastern outpost of the Greco-Roman world, it is the only largely preserved Hellenistic building in the former Soviet Union [1]. The temple is at the edge of a triangular promontory rising above the ravine of the Azat River and the Gegham mountains [1]. It is a part of the fortress of Garni, one of Armenia's oldest, that was strategically significant for the defense of the major cities in the Ararat plain [1]. The entire colonnade collapsed during a devastating earthquake on June 4, 1679, with the epicenter in the Garni Gorge [1]. The structure was rebuilt using its original stones, a technique known as anastylosis [1]. The temple is constructed of locally quarried grey to bluish basalt, assembled without the use of mortar [1].

row.name: Cannington Camp
row.description: Cannington Camp is a univallate hillfort on an isolated 80-metre hilltop near Cannington, Somerset, England [1]. Originally protected by a stone wall with the main entrance to the southeast, the site shows evidence of occupation from the Mesolithic through Roman periods [1] [2] [3]. The site has been proposed as the location of the 878 AD Battle of Cynuit between Viking and Anglo-Saxon forces [1] [4]. The north side has been severely damaged by 19th- and 20th-century limestone quarrying [1] [5].

row.name: Le Grand-Pressigny
row.description: A major Chalcolithic flint mining and production centre in the Indre-et-Loire department of central France, active around 3000 BC during the Final Neolithic [1] [2] [3]. The site produced distinctive caramel-coloured flint of exceptional quality, from which master carvers struck large blades up to 40 cm long that were distributed across Europe to the Alps, Brittany, and Holland [1] [3] [4] [5]. The characteristic products known as livres de beurre are elongated cores from which long flakes were struck [5] [6]. The site is now home to a prehistory museum [2] [5].

row.name: Wanakawri, Cusco
row.description: Wanakawri is an archaeological site and a legendary mountain in Peru [1]. It is situated in the Cusco Region, Cusco Province, in the districts San Jerónimo and San Sebastián, and in the Paruro Province, Yaurisque District [1]. The mountain with the archaeological remains is 4,089 metres high and one of the highest elevations near Cusco [1]. Wanakawri was one of the most important wak'as of the Inca culture [1].

row.name: Lartos, Rhodes
row.description: Lartos was an ancient village on the southeast coast of Rhodes [1]. The site is notable for a major marble formation known as lithos lartios, a distinctive gray-blue stone [1] [2]. This stone was quarried in antiquity for local construction and was likely used for significant architectural projects [1] [2].

row.name: Roman Bath, York
row.description: The ancient remains were uncovered during construction of the current building in 1929–31, which replaced an earlier inn [1]. The pub's exterior features Tudor Revival architecture with applied half-timbering [1] [2]. The Roman bathing complex remains visible inside the building today, offering a rare glimpse into Roman-era York [1] [2] [3].

row.name: Lakhmir Mound
row.description: Lakhmir Mound, locally known as Lakhmir-Ji-Mari, is a Chalcolithic archaeological site in the Naig Valley of Sindh, Pakistan, about 45 km from Sehwan Sharif [1] [2]. The mound consists of two parts: a conical hill and a lower section resembling a town [1] [3]. Archaeologist N.G. Majumdar noted Chalcolithic pottery fragments scattered across the mound and surrounding area, along with embedded stone walls from a prehistoric epoch and black-on-red pottery characteristic of the Indus Valley civilization [1].

row.name: Asine
row.description: An ancient Greek city on the coast of the Argolid, mentioned by Homer in the Iliad as subject to Diomedes of Argos [1]. Habitation spans from the Neolithic through the Bronze Age and into the Early Iron Age [2]. Swedish Crown Prince Gustaf Adolf initiated excavations in 1922, making Asine Sweden's first major fieldwork in Greece [2]. The Barbouna hill yielded a Mycenaean cemetery (c. 1600-1100 BC) with chamber tombs [1] [2].

row.name: Balkerne Gate
row.description: Balkerne Gate is a Roman gateway in Colchester (ancient Camulodunum) [1]. It is the largest surviving gateway in Roman Britain, constructed where the Roman road from Londinium intersected the town wall of Camulodunum [1]. It is a scheduled monument and a Grade I listed building [1].

row.name: Pyramid of Neferhetepes
row.description: The Pyramid of Neferhetepes is a small subsidiary pyramid at Saqqara, built for Queen Neferhetepes, wife of Userkaf, the first king of the Fifth Dynasty [1] [2] [3]. She was the mother of Pharaoh Sahure [1] [2]. First recognized by C. M. Firth in 1928, the pyramid originally stood 16.8 m high with a base of 26.25 m and a slope of 52 degrees [3]. Today it survives only as a mound of rubble with its burial chamber exposed by stone robbers [3].

row.name: Lismore Fields
row.description: Lismore Fields is a prehistoric settlement near the River Wye in Buxton, Derbyshire, discovered in 1984 by the Trent and Peak Archaeological Trust while searching for a Roman road [1]. Excavations revealed two Early Neolithic longhouses, among the best-preserved examples in Britain [2]. Building 1 dates to 3800-3650 BC and Building 2 to 3650-3350 BC [2]. The site yielded one of the largest cereal assemblages from any Early Neolithic site in England, possibly representing the earliest evidence of cereal cultivation in the British Isles [2]. It is a protected Scheduled Monument [1] [2].

row.name: Colebrooke, Devon
row.description: Colebrooke is a village and parish in Devon, England, about 5 miles (8 km) west of Crediton [1]. Remains of a Roman road agger visible in a field roughly 300 metres south of Rag Lane, east of Five Acre Copse [1] [2]. This road maintained its route from North Tawton, becoming less distinct at Colebrooke, though a straight lane along the ridge east of the railway suggests its original line [1].

row.name: Punta de Estaca de Bares
row.description: Punta da Estaca de Bares is the northernmost point of Spain and the Iberian Peninsula, at a latitude of 43° 47′ 38″ North [1]. It is located in Galicia [1]. The peninsula of Estaca de Bares penetrates considerably into the Cantabrian Sea, and as a result it is one of the rainiest places in Europe, with more than 2500 mm a year [1]. These special weather conditions have created over the centuries a unique ecosystem and biodiversity which have made it possible for this area to be declared an Area of National Natural Interest [1]. The ruins of the Phoenician Salt Fish Factory and the Phoenician Port are open to visitors [1].

row.description: Siponto was an ancient port town and bishopric of Magna Graecia in Apulia, southern Italy [1]. Siponto is located around 3 km south of Manfredonia [1]. row.name: Berel Kurgan
row.description: Berel kurgan is an archaeological site in the Katonkaragay District in eastern Kazakhstan [1]. The site is located near the village of Berel [1]. At this site, numerous 5th-3rd century BCE Early Saka kurgans were found [1]. The Kurgans contained vast quantities of precious golden jewelry [1]. Horses were buried in the kurgans next to their owner, and were lavishly decorated [1].

row.name: Uffington White Horse
row.description: The Uffington White Horse is a prehistoric hill figure, 110 m long, formed from deep trenches filled with crushed white chalk [1]. The figure is situated on the upper slopes of Whitehorse Hill in the English civil parish of Uffington in Oxfordshire, some 16 km east of Swindon [1]. The hill forms a part of the scarp of the Berkshire Downs and overlooks the Vale of White Horse to the north [1]. The Uffington White Horse was created some time between 1380 and 550 BC, during the late Bronze Age or early Iron Age [1]. A cartulary of Abingdon Abbey, compiled between 1072 and 1084, refers to "mons albi equi" at Uffington [1]. The most significant nearby feature is the Iron Age Uffington Castle, located on higher ground atop a knoll above the White Horse [1].

row.name: Tarragona
row.description: The real founding date of Tarragona is unknown [1]. During the Roman Republic, the city was fortified and much enlarged as a Roman colony by the brothers Publius Cornelius Scipio and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus, who converted it into a fortress and arsenal against the Carthaginians [1]. The city was first named Colonia Iulia Urbs Triumphalis Tarraco and was capital of the province of Hispania Citerior [1]. Augustus wintered at Tarraco after his Cantabrian campaign, and bestowed many marks of honour on the city, among which were its honorary titles of Colonia Victrix Togata and Colonia Julia Victrix Tarraconensis [1]. According to Mela, it was the richest town on the coast, and Strabo represents its population as equal to that of Carthago Nova [1]. The Roman ruins of Tarraco have been designated a World Heritage Site by UNESCO [1].

row.name: Tower of Elahbel
row.description: The Tower of Elahbel (also known as Tower 13 or Kubbet el 'Arus) was a four-storey sandstone tower tomb near the ancient city of Palmyra in Syria [1]. The tower was one of several built outside the city walls of Palmyra, in an area known as the Valley of the Tombs [1]. The tower was important in the history of textiles: fragments of very early Chinese silk yarns, dated to the 1st century AD, were discovered in the tombs at the tower [1]. The tower was completed in AD103 by a Palmyrene aristocrat Marcus Ulpius Elahbelus and his three brothers, Manai, Shakaiei, and Malku; they were all sons of Wahballat [1].

row.name: Cova Foradà
row.description: Cova Foradà (or Cova Foradada) is an archaeological site consisting of a cave with remains of Neanderthals near Oliva, in the Province of Valencia, Spain [1]. The most complete skeleton of a Neanderthal ever found on the Iberian peninsula was found there in 2010 [1]. The karst cave is located 5 kilometres southeast of the village of Oliva, at 3.5 kilometres from the coast of the Mediterranean, and archaeological excavations have taken place since 1977 [1]. The cave is found in a low hill, one of a group of hills called the Muntanyetes de Oliva, the last part of the Serra de Mustalla before the floodplain that ends at the coast [1]. It has been occupied since the Middle Paleolithic, including in the Mousterian and Mesolithic periods, and in the Bronze Age [1]. A maxilla (almost complete, with a number of teeth), a molar, a fibula, and four fragments of a cranium belonging to two humans were found between 2000 and 2003, in what appeared to be a layer from the Mousterian [1].

row.name: Heraclea Lyncestis
row.description: Heraclea Lyncestis, also transliterated Herakleia Lynkestis, was an ancient Greek city in Macedon, ruled later by the Romans [1]. Its ruins are situated 2 km south of the present-day town of Bitola, North Macedonia [1]. The city was gradually abandoned in the 6th century AD following an earthquake and Slavic invasions [1]. Objects discovered from the time of Roman rule in Heraclea are votive monuments, a portico, thermae (baths), a theatre and town walls [1]. The Roman emperor Hadrian built a theatre in the center of the town, on a hill [1]. In the early Byzantine period (4th to 6th centuries AD) Heraclea was an important episcopal centre [1]. A small and a great basilica, the bishop's residence, and a funerary basilica and the necropolis are some of the remains of this period [1]. Three naves in the Great Basilica are covered with mosaics of very rich floral and figurative iconography; these well preserved mosaics are often regarded as fine examples of the early Christian art period [1].

row.name: Stobi
row.description: Stobi or Stoboi, was an ancient town of Paeonia, later conquered by Macedon, and finally turned into the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia Salutaris [1]. It is located near Gradsko, North Macedonia, on the main road that leads from the Danube to the Aegean Sea [1]. Archeological excavations have shown Stobi was built where the Erigon joins the Axios, making it strategically important as a center for both trade and warfare [1]. Stobi developed from a Paeonian settlement established in the Archaic period [1]. In the reign of Augustus the city grew in size and population [1]. Yugoslavian archaeologists first discovered public and private buildings in the city and then the city's theater, built in the 3rd century, and religious artifacts from the central and western part of the city [1]. In the early Christian period Stobi was an episcopal see by 325, when the bishop Budius took part in the First Council of Nicaea [1]. Stobi is one of a small number of cities from the late antique and early Christian period that kept a large number of mosaics [1].

row.name: Pintia
row.description: Pintia was besieged and destroyed by the Romans, which also buried forever the Vaccean culture, religion, and language [1]. The archaeological excavations conducted in Padilla de Duero uncovered an important settlement that has been interpreted as its possible location [1]. The Archaeological Zone consists of three different parts: the city of Las Quintanas, the necropolis of Las Ruedas, and the potter's district of Carralaceña [1].

row.name: Daskalio
row.description: Daskalio or Dhaskalio is a tiny, uninhabited Greek islet in the Cyclades just off the west coast of the larger island Keros, approximately 150 metres in diameter [1]. Formerly, it was a promontory of Keros, but is now a tiny islet because of sea level rise [1]. Excavation by the Cambridge Keros Project, a joint endeavour of the University of Cambridge, the Ephorate of Antiquities of Cyclades, and the Cyprus Institute, in 2008 revealed a large Bronze Age settlement and ten years later researchers from the university found evidence of advanced metalworking workshops there, dating from 2500 BCE [1]. The island was extensively terraced with over 1,000 tons of marble quarried on the island of Naxos, some 10 km distant, enhancing its pyramidal shape [1]. The lower levels featured a complex drainage system of water conduits, among the oldest in Europe [1]. Plant remains in soil samples included grapes, olives, figs, almonds, emmer wheat and barley, likely imported from more arable locations [1].

row.name: Apidima Cave
row.description: Apidima Cave is a complex of five caves located on the western shore of Mani Peninsula in southern Greece [1]. The scientific research programme at Apidima began in 1978 and is being conducted by the National Archaeological Museum of Greece in collaboration with the Laboratory of Historical Geology-Palaeontology of Athens University [1]. Researchers uncovered two significant fossils in Apidima Cave "A" in 1978 [1]. The two fossils are now referred to as Apidima 1 and Apidima 2 [1]. Research published in July 2019 indicates that the Apidima 2 skull fragment has Neanderthal morphology, and using uranium-thorium dating, was found to be more than 170,000 years old [1]. The Apidima 1 skull fossil was found to be older, dated—using the same method—to more than 210,000 years old [1].

row.name: Taliata
row.description: Taliata was a Roman town and fort located near the present town of Donji Milanovac in eastern Serbia [1]. It is included in the Tabula Peutingeriana [1]. The fort of 134 × 126 m was built as part of the Roman Moesian Limes frontier system of linked forts along the Danube [1]. Domitian replaced the wood and earth walls by stone walls in 87 AD before Domitian's Dacian War [1]. It was completely restored in the second half of the 3rd century [1]. In the 4th c. protruding semicircular corner-towers were added [1]. An early Christian basilica was discovered on the site [1].

row.name: Archaeological Site of La Ribera de Algaida
row.description: The archaeological site of La Ribera de Algaida or Ribera de Turaniana is located in Aguadulce (Almería), Spain and discovered in 1859 [1]. The site is one of the most important human settlements in the history of Almería, Spain, due to its size and long-term occupation [1]. It has an area of 20 to 30 hectares (49 to 74 acres), and was occupied during the late Copper Age (from the Argaric culture until the Roman Era) [1].

row.name: Beacon Hill, West Sussex
row.description: Beacon Hill, also known as Harting Beacon, is a hillfort on the South Downs, in the county of West Sussex in southern England [1]. The hilltop enclosure is dated to the Late Bronze Age, from the 8th to 6th centuries BC [1]. The hillfort defences were renewed during the Late Iron Age [1]. The fort extends approximately 400 metres east-west by approximately 500 metres north-south, and covers an area of approximately 10 hectares [1]. Archaeological investigations of the hillfort took place from 1948 to 1952, and from 1976 to 1977 [1]. As well as the Bronze Age remains, the area of the fort also includes an Anglo-Saxon burial mound, and the foundations of a late 18th-century telegraph station [1]. The hillfort is situated on the top of the hill and is defined by a single rampart and a flat-bottomed ditch, which survives as a low bank up to 6 metres wide [1]. The rampart was originally faced with timber, with timber palisades acting as retaining walls on both the inside and the outside [1].

row.name: Dulan Site
row.description: The Dulan Site (traditional Chinese: 都蘭遺址; simplified Chinese: 都兰遗址; pinyin: Dōulán Yízhǐ) is an archaeological site in Dulan Village, Donghe Township, Taitung County, Taiwan [1]. During Japanese rule of Taiwan, a rectangular stony coffin was excavated in the area [1]. Further investigation by Academia Sinica led to the discovery of a giant stone pile [1]. The site and objects date back to 3,000 years ago [1]. It is now considered a cultural heritage and third grade historical site [1]. The area is divided into two areas, which are the stony coffin area and the stony wall area [1].

row.name: Lindos
row.description: Lindos is an archaeological site in the Dodecanese, Greece [1]. According to myth, Lindos was founded by the Dorians led by the king Tlepolemus of Rhodes, who arrived in about the 10th century BC [1]. It was one of six Dorian cities in the area known as the Dorian Hexapolis [1]. The eastern location of Rhodes made it a natural meeting place between the Greeks and the Phoenicians, and by the 8th century Lindos was a major trading centre [1]. The importance of Lindos declined after the founding of the city of Rhodes in the late 5th century BC [1]. In classical times the acropolis of Lindos was dominated by the massive temple of Athena Lindia, which attained its final form in around 300 BC [1]. Excavations were carried out at Lindos in the years 1900 to 1914 by the Carlsberg Institute of Denmark [1]. The acropolis site was excavated down to bedrock and the foundations of all the buildings were uncovered [1].

row.name: Pushkalavati
row.description: Pushkalavati was the capital of the ancient region of Gandhāra in modern-day northwestern Pakistan [1]. Its ruins are located on the outskirts of the modern city of Charsadda in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, 35–42 kilometres northeast of Peshawar, at the banks of Jindi River [1]. The earliest archaeological remains in Bala Hisar mound are from 1400 to 800 BCE [1]. The ruins of Pushkalavati consist of two sites, separated by the small Shambor river [1]. To the south is Bala Hisar, which consists of two separate mounds, one eastern and one western [1]. To the north is Shaikhan Dheri, wedged between the Shambor and Jindi rivers [1]. According to Arrian, the city then surrendered in 327/326 BCE to Alexander the Great, who established a garrison in it [1].

row.name: Fen Causeway
row.description: Fen Causeway or the Fen Road is the modern name for a Roman road of England that runs between Denver, Norfolk in the east and Peterborough in the west [1]. Its path covers 24 miles, passing March and Eldernell before joining the major Roman north–south route Ermine Street west of modern-day Peterborough [1]. It provided a link from the north and west of England to East Anglia [1]. The road is thought to have been raised above the marshy fens using gravel, with a width of up to 60 feet [1]. Towards its western end it is close to the Bronze Age route across Flag Fen [1].

row.name: Ban Chiang
row.description: Ban Chiang is an archaeological site in Nong Han district, Udon Thani province, Thailand [1]. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992 [1]. Discovered in 1966, the site first attracted interest due to its ancient red-painted pottery [1]. The site's oldest graves do not include bronze artifacts and are therefore from a Neolithic culture; the most recent graves date to the Iron Age [1]. The first intensive excavation of Ban Chiang was a joint effort by the University of Pennsylvania Museum and the Thai Department of Fine Arts [1]. Recovered bronze objects include bracelets, rings, anklets, wires and rods, spearheads, axes and adzes, hooks, blades, and little bells [1]. At least 142 discrete burials were found in the 1974-1975 excavations [1]. Analysis of the human remains by Michael Pietrusewsky and Michele Toomay Douglas revealed that the people lived a vigorous and active lifestyle with little evidence of interpersonal violence or any form of warfare [1].

row.name: Miculla Petroglyphs
row.description: The San Francisco de Miculla petroglyphs, commonly known as the Miculla petroglyphs, are petroglyphs located 22 kilometres from Tacna, Peru [1]. They are carved in low relief in the rocks, and depict people fighting, dancing and hunting animals [1]. They are believed by many to be around 1500 years old, although various people date them from as wide a time period as 500 AD to 1445 AD [1].

row.name: Ourense
row.description: After the Romans, Ourense was part of the Kingdom of the Suebi during most of the 5th, 6th and 7th centuries and was destroyed by the Moors in 716 [1]. It was later rebuilt by Alfonso III of Asturias about 877 [1]. The Norse invasions as well as attacks from the Arab warlord Al-Mansur once more laid the city to waste [1]. The ancient city of Auria is located on both banks of the Miño river in the south-central part of Galicia [1].

row.name: Valley of the Queens
row.description: The Valley of the Queens is a site in Egypt, in which queens, princes, princesses, and other high-ranking officials were buried from roughly 1560 BC to 1130 BC [1]. The Valley of the Queens was known anciently as Ta-Set-Neferu, which has a double meaning of "The Place of Beauty" and/or "the Place of the Royal Children" [1]. Excavation of the tombs at the Valley of the Queens was pioneered by Ernesto Schiaparelli and Francesco Ballerini in the early 1900s [1]. The Valley of the Queens consists of the main wadi, which contains most of the tombs, along with the Valley of Prince Ahmose, the Valley of the Rope, the Valley of the Three Pits, and the Valley of the Dolmen [1]. The main wadi contains 91 tombs and the subsidiary valleys add another 19 tombs [1]. The burials in the subsidiary valleys all date to the 18th Dynasty [1]. The Valley was no longer a royal burial site after the close of the 20th Dynasty [1]. Not much is known about the use of the Valley of the Queens during the Ptolemaic Period but during the Roman Period there was a renewed, extensive use of the Valley as a burial site [1].

row.name: Alphen aan den Rijn
row.description: The area around Alphen aan den Rijn has been inhabited for 2000 years [1]. In the Roman era, the Oude Rijn was the main branch of the Rhine River and formed the north border of the Roman Empire [1]. Since the rule of Emperor Claudius (41–54 AD), divisions of the Roman army were stationed here [1]. Consequently, several Roman fortifications were located along the Oude Rijn, including castellum Albanianae in the centre of Alphen [1]. The Romans had also built the first bridge over the Oude Rijn [1]. Alphen was therefore an important commercial site in the area until Germanic raids ended that in 240 AD [1].

row.name: Multan Fort
row.description: The Multan Fort was a historic fort in the city of Multan, Punjab, Pakistan [1]. It was built on a hillock separated from the city by the Ravi River [1]. The fort was destroyed in 1849 by British forces during the Second Anglo-Sikh War [1]. The walls of the fort were built by the Mughal prince Murad Bakhsh in the 17th century [1]. The famed Multan Sun Temple was located within the fort premises [1]. Contemporary reports put the walls of the fort at 40 to 70 feet high and 6,800 feet in circumference [1]. The fort had 46 bastions which included two flanking towers at each of the four gates [1].

row.name: Nîmes
row.description: The Neolithic site of Serre Paradis reveals the presence of semi-nomadic cultivators in the period 4000 to 3500 BCE on the site of Nîmes [1]. The hill of Mt. Cavalier was the site of the early oppidum, which gave birth to the city [1]. The Greek geographer, Strabo, mentioned that this town functioned as the regional capital for the Volcae Arecomici, a Celtic people [1]. Nîmes became a Roman colony as Colonia Nemausus sometime before 28 BCE, as witnessed by the earliest coins [1]. Augustus launched a major construction program in the city [1]. Additionally, he ordered the construction of a 6 kilometres long ring of ramparts in the city, reinforced by 14 towers; two gates remain today: the Porte d'Auguste, and the Porte de France [1]. The Maison Carrée, a small Roman temple dedicated to sons of Agrippa was built c. 19 BCE [1].

row.name: Antequera Dolmens Site
row.description: The Antequera Dolmens Site is a cultural heritage ensemble comprising three cultural monuments (the Dolmen of Menga, Dolmen of Viera and Tholos of El Romeral) and 2 natural mountain features (the Peña de los Enamorados and El Torcal) in and near the city of Antequera in Andalusia, Spain [1]. The cultural institution responsible for its protection is the CADA [1]. It was declared a World Heritage Site in 2016 [1]. Both the Dolmen of Menga and the Tholos of El Romeral have anomalous orientations [1]. The archaeoastronomer Michael Hoskin, who studied the site, noted that, whereas the axes of almost all dolmens around the Mediterranean are oriented to a celestial feature, such as sunrise at dawn on the equinoxes (as occurs in the Dolmen of Viera), the Dolmen of Menga points to the striking nearby peak called the Peña de los Enamorados [1]. This rises abruptly from the plain and contains the contemporaneous rock shelter of Matacabras, in which cave paintings are found [1].

row.name: Zafarraya
row.description: Zafarraya is known for a Neanderthal mandible found in a cave in 1983 by Cecilio Barroso and Paqui Medina [1]. The mandible has been dated to 30,000 years Before Present (BP), and at the time represented the youngest-known Neanderthal remains [1]. Near the mandible, Mousterian tools dated to 27,000 years BP were found [1]. The find was one of the first pieces of definite evidence showing that the presence of Neanderthals and modern humans overlapped in Europe for a significant period [1].

row.name: Roman Emperors Route
row.description: The Roman Emperors Route is a tourism and archaeology project in Serbia, a route spanning 600 km with several ancient Roman sites, among which are notable cities, estates and birthplaces [1]. The project's name is derived from the fact that 17 Roman emperors were born within the current borders of Serbia [1]. The sites include the important Roman cities of Sirmium, Felix Romuliana and Naissus [1].

row.old_value: 1000-1500 AD archaeological park in the San Sebastian District, on the Pumamarka river. Declared National Cultural Heritage -- an Inca-era site in the heart of the Cusco Region.
A Greek colony of Syracuse in the 4th century BC. Its ruins were still visible to Renaissance travelers before vanishing under farmland.
4th-millennium BC site on north Anglesey. The surrounding landscape holds Neolithic remains from one of the earliest-settled coastal zones on this part of the island.
Maya pyramids, plazas, and a ball court occupied from 200 BC to 1100 AD on the Yucatan coast. Its position made it a trading hub connecting coastal and inland networks for over a millennium.
A settlement spanning the 1st millennium BC to the 5th century AD. Its long habitation record makes it a rare window into how rural life changed through the Iron Age and Roman period.
A village where a Scordisci Celtic settlement was found. The Scordisci were a fierce Celtic tribe who raided as far south as Delphi before Rome subdued them.
Dating to the 4th century at Ras — medieval capital of the Grand Principality of Rascia — this is the oldest intact church in the country. Additions came as late as the 7th century.
25th-24th century BC pyramid at Abusir, likely built for a wife of King Nyuserre Ini. The largely destroyed 5th Dynasty Double Pyramid stands east of the Neferefre pyramid in the Abusir field.
A Roman villa near Pompeii with storage rooms where 20 bodies were found huddled together during the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD.
row.new_value: The garden side of the building faces what would have been the ancient coast line to the East.

row.old_value: Home to the only known Roman villa or high-status farmhouse in the entire county. Bronze Age remains from the 12th century BC underlie the Roman layers.
A treasury building at Olympia where the city-state of Megara stored its offerings to Zeus. Treasuries like this lined the sacred way, each city competing to display its wealth.
Bronze Age settlement in Lower Silesia with occupation continuing into the Early Middle Ages. Stobno has archaeological sites from both eras; first recorded in writing in 1259 under Piast dynastic.
1000–1500 AD. Mawk'allaqta in Sandia Province sits in cloud-forest highlands — a National Heritage site named 'old town' in Quechua, echoing the people who once built and lived here.
500–900 AD. Hidden along the Cotahuasi Canyon, Marpa preserves Inca road segments, agricultural terraces, staircases, and ancient tombs barely explored by anyone before 1994.
A 55 m pyramid built around 1991 BC by the founder of the Twelfth Dynasty. Its core reused blocks stripped from older Old Kingdom pyramids.
Built atop an earlier structure when the city was Caesarodunum, this 1st-century AD arena once seated 34,000 spectators before its ruins were folded into the medieval city walls.
1st-century AD Roman city at Feldkirch on the Tabula Peutingeriana, a waystation between Brigantium and Milan. Geophysics in 1998 confirmed it was Vorarlberg's second largest Roman settlement.
A skull unearthed in 1940 proved nearly 15,000 years old; later digs found hearths from 29,000 BC. Keilor is one of the earliest habitation sites on the continent; megafauna remains suggest hunting.
The only standing Greco-Roman colonnaded building in the Caucasus, built as a temple to the sun god Mihr. Its Ionic columns follow a style originating in the 7th century BC.
A Bronze and Iron Age hillfort that is roughly square with a single rampart enclosing 5 hectares. Cliff erosion on the north side has eaten into the defences.
Agricultural terraces 4 km north of Zurite in the Anta Province of Cusco. The terracing system is one of hundreds that transformed Andean hillsides into productive land under Inca engineering.
A Neolithic flint mine producing a prized caramel-coloured stone traded across Europe. Finished tools from this quarry have turned up as far away as the Netherlands and the Pyrenees.
5th-century BC village on the southeast coast of Rhodes, source of a distinctive gray-blue marble, lithos lartios, quarried in antiquity for local use and still characteristic of the island.
A 1st-century military bathhouse 15 feet underground, complete with tepidarium, caldarium, and frigidarium. Tiles stamped with legion identities suggest the Ninth Legion built it.
A conical mound from around 3000 BC with a lower section that resembles a planned town. It dates to the same era as the great Indus Valley cities.
A Mycenaean city mentioned by Homer that was destroyed by neighboring Argos in the 8th century BC. The survivors were resettled in Messenia — forced exile as geopolitics.
A 1st-century AD Roman gateway in ancient Camulodunum (Colchester), the first capital of Roman Britain. It is the largest surviving Roman gateway in the country.

1st-5th century AD site on Mount Pirwayuq at 3,900 m in Tayacaja Province, Huancavelica Region. A high Andean summit site in the Laria District, marking pre-Inca occupation of remote mountain terrain.
A small queen's pyramid built just 10 m south of Userkaf's own, dating to the 25th century BC. Queens got their own mini pyramid complexes.
Timber post-holes at this Buxton site date to around 5000 BC, preserving rectangular Neolithic buildings. Charred grain here is among the earliest direct evidence of farming in the north.
A hamlet where the remains of a Roman road's raised embankment can still be traced across fields. The road connected two Roman towns along a ridge of hills.
An ancient port town from the 3rd century BC abandoned after earthquakes in the 13th century. Legend says it was founded by the Greek hero Diomedes.
row.new_value: Siponto was an ancient port town and bishopric of Magna Graecia in Apulia. In 189 BC it became a Roman colony with the name Sipontum.

row.old_value: 3rd century BC to 2nd century AD -- 24 rock-cut caves on the Trivashmi Hills, excavated by Jain saints. Monasteries, shrines, cisterns, pillars, and Hinayana Buddhist carvings fill the system.
A fort whose original construction may date to 1000-800 BC, rebuilt many times by successive rulers. British colonial forces destroyed it, leaving only fragments of its long history.
row.new_value: The walls of the fort were built by the Mughal prince Murad Bakhsh in the 17th century.

row.old_value: A cave where a Neanderthal jawbone dated to 28,000 BC was found alongside Mousterian tools. At the time, it was the youngest-known Neanderthal specimen ever identified.
row.new_value: Zafarraya is known for a Neanderthal mandible found in a cave in 1983 by Cecilio Barroso and Paqui Medina.

row.old_value: Founded by Philip II near modern Bitola, this ancient city became an Episcopal seat on the Via Egnatia. Its 5th-6th century floor mosaics rank with the finest in the Balkans.
row.new_value: Objects discovered from the time of Roman rule in Heraclea are votive monuments, a portico, thermae, a theatre and town walls.

row.old_value: Known in antiquity as Ta-Set-Neferu — "the place of beauty" — this necropolis across five valleys holds 110 royal tombs. Nefertari's tomb contains wall paintings of extraordinary preservation.
row.new_value: Excavation of the tombs at the Valley of the Queens was pioneered by Ernesto Schiaparelli and Francesco Ballerini in the early 1900s.

row.old_value: Three 3rd-millennium BC megalithic monuments dominate this UNESCO site — led by the Menga dolmen, whose capstone weighs 180 tonnes and was hauled into place without any machinery.
row.new_value: The Antequera Dolmens Site is a cultural heritage ensemble comprising three cultural monuments and 2 natural mountain features in and near the city of Antequera in Andalusia.

row.old_value: Dubbed the most Roman city outside Italy, it has the best-preserved Roman arena and the Maison Carree temple. Neolithic habitation dates to 4000 BC.
A tiny Cycladic islet once connected to Keros, separated by rising seas. Thousands of deliberately broken figurines were deposited here as votive offerings.
A burial site where a rectangular stone coffin was found during Japanese-era rule. Giant stone piles and artifacts date to the 2nd millennium BC.
1st-century AD Roman road, 39 km across the Fens from Denver, Norfolk to Peterborough. Fen Causeway linked East Anglia to the north and west, joining Ermine Street at its western end.

row.old_value: Ancient Cretan city-state listed by the Byzantine geographer Hierocles among 22 cities of Crete. Positioned 170 stadia from Hierapytna, it appears in myths tied to Otus and Ephialtes.
Covering 0.84 hectares in Somerset's Selwood parish, this univallate hillfort retains a bank up to 1.6 m high with a 1.8 m ditch below it. It sits close to the later Hales Castle.
Northernmost tip of the peninsula, where Phoenician salt fish factory ruins and a Phoenician port survive. A lighthouse raised in 1850 still operates on the same headland.
A Roman Danubian fort (134 x 126 m) in the Moesian Limes frontier system. Its walls were upgraded from wood to stone before Domitian's Dacian War in 87 AD.
A Roman fort from the 1st century AD on the Rhine frontier. The river was the empire's edge — legionaries here watched the border every day for 200 years.

Zafarraya is known for a Neanderthal mandible found in a cave in 1983 by Cecilio Barroso and Paqui Medina.
A common with two saucer-shaped Bronze Age round barrows, now both a Scheduled Monument and an SSSI. The barrows are the low, dish-like type used for cremation burials.

row.old_value: Siponto was an ancient port town and bishopric of Magna Graecia in Apulia. In 189 BC it became a Roman colony with the name Sipontum.
Spanning 20–30 hectares, this site was inhabited from the Copper Age through the Roman era — one of the longest-occupied settlements in the Almería region, first found in 1859.
A hilltop enclosure from the Late Bronze Age whose defences were renewed in the Late Iron Age. The single rampart and ditch protected a settlement for centuries.
Capital of ancient Gandhara from 1400 BC, later an Achaemenid regional capital. Alexander the Great's army passed through here during its march into the Indian subcontinent.
500-1445 AD. Carved 22 km from Tacna - fighting, dancing, and hunting scenes in low relief. Spanning nearly a thousand years of carving, Miculla ranks among the most-visited rock art in the region.
A 600 km tourism route linking the birthplaces and estates of 18 Roman emperors. More Roman emperors came from this region than any other outside Italy.
At 4,089 meters near Cusco, Wanakawri was the most sacred wak'a in the Inca religious system — central to founding myths and visited in major state rituals from 1438 until the Spanish conquest.
Saka kurgans from the 5th-3rd century BC that contained golden jewelry and horses buried beside their owners. Permafrost preserved organic materials in extraordinary detail.
A 110-meter-long horse figure from ~1000 BC, carved by filling trenches with crushed white chalk. It must be re-scoured every few decades or the grass reclaims it.
A four-story sandstone tower tomb built in 103 AD outside Palmyra's city walls. Tower tombs like this could hold hundreds of burials in stacked compartments.
Karst cave near Oliva where the most complete Neanderthal skeleton ever found on the Iberian Peninsula was excavated in 2010. Archaeological work has continued here since 1977.
A Roman crossroads city where the Crna meets the Vardar. Stobi was capital of Macedonia Salutaris and a strategic center for trade and military campaigns.

row.old_value: One of the three ancient city-states of Rhodes, founded according to myth by Danaus. Its dramatic acropolis holds a temple to Athena Lindia rebuilt after a fire in 342 BC.
A settlement with 4,000 years of continuous use, famous for its vivid red-painted pottery. Bronze tools found here rewrote the timeline of Southeast Asian metallurgy.
A city known since Roman times for its hot springs, called the Burgas. It remains one of the European cities with the greatest thermal heritage.
The walls of the fort were built by the Mughal prince Murad Bakhsh in the 17th century.
Roman Tarraco was capital of Hispania Tarraconensis, the largest province in the west. Cyclopean wall bases near the old prison predate the Romans, belonging to an earlier 5th-century BC settlement.
A Vaccaean city, part of an early Celtic society in northern Iberia. The Vaccaei were the first sedentary people of the Duero-Pisuerga valley.
Karstic sea cliff housing one of Europe’s most significant Palaeolithic cave sites. Accessible only by boat today — during the ice ages, the sea level stood more than 100 metres lower.

row.old_value: Excavation of the tombs at the Valley of the Queens was pioneered by Ernesto Schiaparelli and Francesco Ballerini in the early 1900s.
Iron Age hill fort crowning Long Mountain at 408 metres, possibly crossed by a Roman road linking Wroxeter to Forden Gaer. The summit lies within one country while the mountain straddles two.

On the Pumamarka River in Peru's Cusco Region, Pumamarka is an archaeological park whose Aymara and Quechua name means puma village, and a National Cultural Heritage of Peru.
Hierocles lists Biannus among the 22 cities of Crete, and its Hellenistic coins survive. On a hill northwest of modern Viannos, remains run from the Orientalizing period to Roman times.
In the parish of Selwood, Somerset, Roddenbury Hillfort is a univallate Iron Age hillfort covering 0.84 hectares, a Scheduled Monument that stood on the Heritage at Risk Register in 2011.
On Sicily's southeast coast, Helorus was a Greek colony of Syracuse founded in the late 8th century BC. Among them the Colonna Pizzuta, a 10.5-metre column from the 3rd century BC.
Near the village of Tregele in northern Anglesey stands the Llanfechell Cromlech, where Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age rock art was found on one of its stones in 2004-2005.
Chacchoben, a Maya ruin approximately 177 km south of Tulum in Quintana Roo, Mexico, means Place of Red Maize in Maya. INAH began restoration in 1994; in 2002 the site opened to the public.
Walton Common, a 25.5 hectare Site of Special Scientific Interest, holds two saucer-shaped Bronze Age round barrows and a late Iron Age banjo enclosure that may be a univallate hillfort.
Alverdiscott, a village and civil parish in Torridge, Devon, England, 9 km south-south-west of Barnstaple, holds a Scheduled Ancient Monument: a Roman marching camp.
South of the river Vuka and northwest of Vinkovci in eastern Croatia, Markušica gave up a Scordisci site of the Late La Tene culture, dug in rescue work of the 1970s and 1980s.
Excavations beneath the floor of the Church of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul at Ras uncovered black-figure pottery from the 7th-6th centuries BC and a 5th-century BC princely grave.
On the southeastern edge of the Abusir necropolis, the Lepsius No.25 Pyramid is a 5th Dynasty double tomb: the eastern tomb measures 27.7 by 21.5 m, and lacked a mortuary temple.
Outside the walls of Pompeii, the Villa of Diomedes stands on two levels around 3500 square meters, facing what would have been the ancient coast line, though it is not clear it was his.
Roman occupation at Keal Cotes runs from the 1st to 4th century AD. A 1960s field walk uncovered tessellated mosaic floor tiles; ploughing has left only cropmarks, visible from the air.
The Megarian Treasury at Olympia held the votive offerings of Megara: built mainly from limestone, with a roof of terracotta tiles, statues, limestone reliefs and carvings in cedarwood.
Stobno was settled in prehistoric times: Bronze Age and Early Middle Age sites lie nearby, and the village is first written in 1259, in Piast-ruled Poland since the late 10th century.
Mawk'allaqta, an archaeological settlement in southeastern Peru's Puno Region, was declared a National Cultural Heritage by the country's National Institute of Culture.
Marpa's ruins straddle both sides of the river in the Cotahuasi Canyon, around 3,400 metres deep. The Inca road may follow an older route built by the Wari culture, circa 500-900 AD.
The Pyramid of Amenemhat I at el-Lisht, built by the founder of the Twelfth Dynasty who moved the capital from Thebes to Itj-tawy, now stands at approximately 20 m.
The Tours Amphitheatre stands behind the cathedral in Tours, France, a Roman amphitheatre of the 1st century AD. In front of the Roman amphitheatre, the cathedral stands.
Clunia, an ancient Roman city in present-day Feldkirch, Vorarlberg, Austria, is marked on the Tabula Peutingeriana as a settlement along the Roman road network. The map still names it.
In 1940 a cranium nearly 15,000 years old came to light at the Keilor Archaeological Site. Hearths about 31,000 years BP; megafauna remains suggest a possible Aboriginal hunting link.
Built in the Ionic order, the colonnade of the Garni Temple fell in the earthquake of June 4, 1679 and was rebuilt from its own stones, without mortar, in grey to bluish basalt.
On an isolated 80-metre hilltop, Cannington Camp is a univallate hillfort occupied from the Mesolithic through Roman periods. It is proposed as the site of the 878 AD Battle of Cynuit.
The terraces of Quriwayrachina, an archaeological site also called Quri Wayrachina, step across Peru's Cusco Region in Anta Province, about 4 km north of the terraces of Zurite.
At Le Grand-Pressigny, carvers struck blades up to 40 cm long from caramel-coloured flint and sent them to the Alps, Brittany and Holland. The mines were active around 3000 BC.
Wanakawri is a legendary mountain and an archaeological site at 4,089 metres, one of the highest elevations near Cusco. It was one of the most important wak'as of the Inca culture.
On the southeast coast of Rhodes stands Lartos, an ancient village notable for a major marble formation: lithos lartios, a distinctive gray-blue stone quarried in antiquity.
The Roman Bath in York was uncovered in 1929–31 while the present building rose over an earlier inn. Its Roman bathing complex is still visible inside, a rare glimpse of Roman-era York.
Lakhmir Mound rises in the Naig Valley of Sindh as a conical hill above a lower section resembling a town, where black-on-red pottery of the Indus Valley civilization lies scattered.
On the Argolid coast, Asine is the city the Iliad of Homer gives to Diomedes of Argos. In 1922 Swedish Crown Prince Gustaf Adolf began excavations, Sweden's first major fieldwork in Greece.
At ancient Camulodunum in Colchester, Balkerne Gate is the largest surviving gateway in Roman Britain, built where the Roman road from Londinium met the town wall.
Atop Mount Pirwayuq, the site of Pirwayuq sits at approximately 3,900 meters above sea level, in the Laria District of Tayacaja Province in the Huancavelica Region.
At Saqqara, stone robbers have left the Pyramid of Neferhetepes a mound of rubble with its burial chamber exposed: it once stood 16.8 m high, built for the wife of Userkaf.
Searching for a Roman road in 1984, the Trent and Peak Archaeological Trust uncovered two Early Neolithic longhouses at Lismore Fields, among the best-preserved in Britain.
At Colebrooke, Devon, the agger of a Roman road still shows in a field roughly 300 metres south of Rag Lane. It fades near the village, yet a straight lane along the ridge suggests its line.
The northernmost point of Spain, Punta da Estaca de Bares reaches into the Cantabrian Sea and takes more than 2500 mm of rain a year, one of the rainiest places in Europe.
About 3 km south of Manfredonia, Siponto was a port town and bishopric of Magna Graecia. In 189 BC it became the Roman colony Sipontum; in 663 AD the Slavs took and destroyed it.
Near the village of Berel in eastern Kazakhstan, Berel Kurgan holds numerous 5th-3rd century BCE Early Saka kurgans, vast quantities of golden jewelry, and horses buried beside their owners.
Cut into the upper slopes of Whitehorse Hill in Oxfordshire, the Uffington White Horse runs 110 m in trenches of crushed white chalk, made between 1380 and 550 BC.
No one knows when Tarragona was first founded. The Scipio brothers turned it into a fortress and arsenal against the Carthaginians; Mela called it the richest town on the coast.
Outside the city walls of Palmyra, in the Valley of the Tombs, stood the Tower of Elahbel. In its tombs were found fragments of very early Chinese silk yarns dated to the 1st century AD.
Cova Foradà, a cave in a low hill near Oliva, gave up a maxilla and fragments of a cranium. In 2010 came the most complete Neanderthal skeleton ever found on the Iberian peninsula.
At Heraclea Lyncestis, the Roman emperor Hadrian built a theatre on a hill. In the Great Basilica, three naves are covered with mosaics of very rich floral and figurative iconography.
Stobi stands near Gradsko, where the Erigon joins the Axios, on the road from the Danube to the Aegean. Its theatre was built in the 3rd century, and it kept a large number of mosaics.
Pintia was besieged and destroyed by the Romans, and with it went the Vaccean culture, religion and language. The zone has three parts: a city, a necropolis and a potter's district.
Daskalio, a tiny islet off Keros in the Cyclades, was once a promontory before the sea rose. Metalworking workshops dating from 2500 BCE were found there, and Naxos marble terraces it.
Five caves on the western shore of the Mani Peninsula make up Apidima Cave. Apidima 2, with Neanderthal morphology, was dated to more than 170,000 years; Apidima 1 is older.
Taliata was a Roman fort on the Moesian Limes, the chain of forts along the Danube. Domitian gave its wood and earth walls stone faces in 87 AD; an early Christian basilica was found there.
At Aguadulce in Almería, the site of La Ribera de Algaida covers 20 to 30 hectares and was occupied from the Argaric culture until the Roman Era. It was discovered in 1859.
On top of a South Downs hill, the Beacon Hill fort is a single rampart and a flat-bottomed ditch, now a low bank up to 6 metres wide. The area also holds an Anglo-Saxon burial mound.
In Dulan Village, the Dulan Site holds a rectangular stony coffin, dug during Japanese rule, and a giant stone pile found by Academia Sinica. Its objects date back to 3,000 years ago.
On Rhodes in the Dodecanese, the acropolis of Lindos was dominated by the massive temple of Athena Lindia, which attained its final form around 300 BC, and was excavated down to bedrock.
The ruins of Pushkalavati are two sites, Bala Hisar to the south and Shaikhan Dheri to the north. According to Arrian, the city surrendered in 327/326 BCE to Alexander the Great.
Across the fens, the Fen Causeway runs 24 miles from Denver to Peterborough, thought raised on gravel up to 60 feet wide. Near its western end lies the Bronze Age route across Flag Fen.
Red-painted pottery drew the first interest in Ban Chiang in 1966. At least 142 burials were dug in 1974-1975, giving up bracelets, rings, anklets, spearheads and little bells.
Low-relief carvings cut into the rocks 22 kilometres from Tacna show people fighting, dancing and hunting animals. Many believe the Miculla Petroglyphs are around 1500 years old.
On both banks of the Miño river sits Ourense, ancient Auria. The Moors destroyed it in 716; Alfonso III of Asturias rebuilt it about 877, and Al-Mansur's attacks laid it to waste again.
Queens, princes and high-ranking officials were buried in the Valley of the Queens from roughly 1560 BC to 1130 BC. The ancients called it Ta-Set-Neferu, the Place of Beauty.
About 8 km south of Nashik lie the Pandavleni Caves, a Buddhist and Jain site. Most are viharas, monasteries, save Cave 18, a chaitya prayer hall from the 1st century BCE.
Beacon Ring's summit stands at 408 metres within Wales, on a hill straddling the Powys and Shropshire boundary. A tree plantation covers the site, and its EIIR monogram makes it famous.
Along the Oude Rijn, the north border of the Roman Empire, stood Alphen aan den Rijn: Roman forts, the first bridge over the river, and a busy trade that ended in 240 AD.
On a hillock across the Ravi from the city, Multan Fort's walls rose 40 to 70 feet high around 46 bastions. The Mughal prince Murad Bakhsh built them in the 17th century.

Before Nîmes was the Roman colony of Colonia Nemausus, semi-nomadic cultivators worked its Neolithic site of Serre Paradis from 4000 to 3500 BCE. Augustus ringed the city with ramparts.
Almost all dolmens around the Mediterranean are oriented to a celestial feature. At the Antequera Dolmens Site, the Dolmen of Menga points instead at the nearby Peña de los Enamorados.
In 1983 Cecilio Barroso and Paqui Medina found a Neanderthal mandible in a cave at Zafarraya, dated to 30,000 years BP. Mousterian tools lay near it, dated to 27,000 years BP.
The Roman Emperors Route spans 600 km across Serbia, through the Roman cities of Sirmium, Felix Romuliana and Naissus, in a land where 17 Roman emperors were born.
